_about: Names for Karateka's routines and globals, with the evidence for each.
This file exists because `recovered/karateka.asm` is gitignored and must
stay so -- a byte-identical reconstruction is the game. What can be kept
is the *reading*: addresses, names, and why. Run tools/annotate.py to
apply these to a freshly generated listing and get source that still
reassembles to the original, byte for byte.
Addresses are image offsets. Add 0x200 for a file offset. Globals are
offsets from DS, which the entry stub sets to image + 0x6CA0.
`why` is not decoration. A name with no evidence behind it is a guess
that will be believed by the next reader, and this project has already
published three of those and had to withdraw them.

_unnamed: Nothing is unnamed. Every one of the 120 routine prologues and every one of
the 312 data-segment addresses the code references -- 1,642 references, all
of them -- carries a name and the evidence for it.
That number is only meaningful with the caveats attached, so here they are:
* The names are not equally strong. Each `why` says which kind of evidence
it rests on -- a probe four cases agreed on, an argument watched during a
real run, a body that states it outright, or a single reader. The last is
the weakest and there are a lot of them.
* A great many were never separate variables at all. DS:0x0337 is one
16,000-byte off-screen frame and forty 'globals' were rows of it; another
sixteen are elements of tables whose extents were established separately.
Folding those was arithmetic, not judgement.
* Six were named wrongly first. 'Read by play_sound, never written,
therefore a sound table' is a plausible inference and it made the closing
credits into tune data. The reader tells you who uses an address; only
the bytes tell you what is in it.
What is still not here is a *C* reconstruction. This is assembly that
reassembles to the original exactly, which is a different and stronger claim
about the bytes and a weaker one about the design. Lattice C 2.1 would be
needed for the other, and the copy on this machine is 3.10 with no library.
_globals_note: 199 of the 312 data-segment addresses the code names are named above --
64% of them, and 89% of every reference, because what is left is thin.
113 remain and 94 are referenced twice or fewer. Two uses give two data
points and no shape: not enough to tell a flag from a counter, let alone
what it counts. Naming them would produce names the next reader believes,
which this project has had to undo three times already.
The single finding that moved this most was not a naming technique at all.
DS:0x0337 is a 16,000-byte off-screen CGA frame -- 200 rows of 80 -- and it
ends at 0x4217, exactly where the blitter's own globals begin. Forty of the
addresses that looked like separate variables were rows inside it, which is
why they were only ever written with 0x5555 and 0x2055: those are pixels.
A `[di + 0x337]` in the listing is not a global with a displacement. It is
_confirmed_by_library: Lattice C 2.12 for DOS (1984) was fetched and scanned against this image
with libscan.py. It matched 3 modules of 625 -- 0.2% -- and that number
understates what it settled: the three carry seven symbols, and all seven
land on addresses already named here from behaviour alone. Seven for seven.
The 0.2% is explained, not disappointing. Karateka names Lattice C **2.1**
and the obtainable release is **2.12**; the library was rebuilt between
those point releases, so most modules differ by a byte or two and an
exact-bytes scan refuses them -- correctly. The three that matched are the
small ones nobody had reason to change.
The memory model is **D**, not S: LCS.LIB matched nothing and LCD.LIB
matched all three. That agrees with the entry stub setting DS once to a
segment of its own while code is addressed from zero.
What this does *not* give is a recompile. There is no C source for
Karateka; producing one that compiles to identical bytes is the extended-
reconstruction workflow, measured in weeks. What the library gives is
